newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown weakens but intervention seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown weakens but intervention seen unlikely.

text.p: The Czech crown weakened some 40 basis points against its dollar/mark basket on Wednesday as the market digested central bank comments that the currency was too strong and the bank was considering how to react.
However, analysts and dealers said the Czech National Bank (CNB)'s room for intervention to influence the crown was limited if it was to avoid damage to the overheating economy.
CNB board member Jiri Pospisil said on Tuesday the bank was prepared to intervene to prevent the crown strengthening further, either through interest rates or direct intervention.

"The central bank would be most happy if it didn't have to do anything but unfortunately for the CNB the statement influenced the market only for a day or even a few hours," said Zivnostenska Banka chief analyst Pavel Sobisek.
The CNB fixed the crown at 28.45 to the dollar and 16.696 to the mark at 1046 GMT, 3.45 percent above parity, after an early 28.464 to the dollar or 3.89 percent above parity.
Dealers said the market was highly illiquid.

The crown has been one of Eastern Europe's most stable currencies. It reached record highs in late January and early February, fuelled by demand after a wave of nearly 40 billion crowns of Eurobond issues since the start of the year.
Foreign investors have also been taking advantage of wide interest rate differentials against other currencies.
Sobisek said the bank was hoping the situation would resolve itself and some analysts have said the Eurobond wave, at least, has peaked.
"If it takes too long some action will probably be necessary but it is really difficult to guess which alternative would be less harmful for the CNB and for the Czech Republic," Sobisek said.

Cutting interest rates would boost the money supply and inflation, particularly as the government was considering price deregulation which Sobisek said could add three to four percentage points to inflation alone.
Direct intervention to drive the crown down would be costly and could lead to a counter-effect and further capital inflows.
Komercni Banka dealer Jan Strubek said there was no central bank intervention on Wednesday and that he did not expect any.
"There was no direct intervention and I think it moved only with the proclamation of the CNB board member," he said.
"The comments of the central bank are strong enough to move the market. Especially foreign investors are very sensitive to CNB proclamations," he added.
Jonathan Garner, director of strategy for emerging Europe, Middle East and Africa at Robert Fleming Securities in London said the Czech authorities faced a policy dilemma.

In seeking to curb the high domestic demand, which was at the root of the overheating problem visible in a ballooning trade deficit, through a tight monetary policy, they risked creating problems for the exchange rate.
"The answer isn't to cut interest rates to deal with the overvalued exchange rate...the key problem is in overheating and domestic consumption." Garner said.

He said the CNB should maintain its tight monetary policy, which was showing some signs of dampening domestic demand, and consider administrative measures, as used in some fast-growing Asian economies, to check foreign capital inflows.
The CNB has not intervened since last February when it propped up the crown after widening the fixing corridor to plus/minus 7.5 percent against the basket from 0.5 percent.
The CNB's repo rate remains 12.4 percent, while its discount rate has been at 10.5 percent since last June.
